usage: 뒤늦게 = belatedly; super common with 깨닫다 when the realization comes after the fact
I only just realized it now
이제야 = only now; what you say when something finally clicks
examples: 지갑을 두고 온 걸 지하철에서 깨달았어요.
I realized on the subway that I'd left my wallet behind.
V-(으)ㄴ 걸 깨닫다 = realize that you V-ed; the most useful pattern for this verb
한국에 살면서 매운 걸 잘 먹는다는 걸 깨달았어요.
Living in Korea, I realized I'm actually good with spicy food.
-는다는 걸 깨닫다 reports a realization about a present habit or fact
실수한 걸 깨닫고 바로 사과했어요.
I realized my mistake and apologized right away.
깨닫고 = realized and then; 깨달아요 has ㄷ→ㄹ before a vowel
nuance: 깨닫다 is a sudden realization or dawning understanding, not the gradual 'getting it' of 이해하다. It's the moment a fact clicks into place, often something you should have noticed earlier. Watch the ㄷ irregular: the ㄷ becomes ㄹ before a vowel (깨달아요, 깨달았어요, 깨달으세요) but stays ㄷ before a consonant (깨닫고, 깨닫지).
mistakes: Writing 깨닫아요 instead of 깨달아요 — the ㄷ must change to ㄹ before the -아요 vowel ending

usage: what you say when a memory or idea pops up out of nowhere
A good idea came to me
생각이 떠오르다 = an idea occurs to you; the idea is the subject, marked with 이/가
examples: 그 사람 이름이 갑자기 안 떠올라요.
I suddenly can't remember that person's name.
이름이 안 떠오르다 = a name won't come to mind; the natural way to say 'it's on the tip of my tongue'
이 노래를 들으면 고향이 떠올라요.
When I hear this song, my hometown comes to mind.
N이/가 떠오르다 — the thing that surfaces in your mind takes the subject marker
회의 중에 좋은 아이디어가 떠올랐어요.
A good idea came to me during the meeting.
떠올랐어요 shows the 르 irregular: 르 → ㄹㄹ, so 떠오르 + 았 → 떠올랐
nuance: 떠오르다 is intransitive — thoughts, memories, names, and ideas 'rise up' into your mind on their own (생각이 떠올라요). It literally means 'to float up,' so it's also used for the sun rising. Don't confuse it with the transitive 떠올리다 (to call something to mind on purpose); with 떠오르다 the idea is the subject, not the object.
mistakes: Saying 생각을 떠올라요 with 을/를 — 떠오르다 is intransitive, so it must be 생각이 떠올라요 (use 떠올리다 if you want an object)

usage: the go-to phrase when something is mixing you up; softer than 모르겠어요
Don't get confused / Don't mix them up
a friendly warning when two things look or sound alike
examples: 왼쪽이랑 오른쪽이 항상 헷갈려요.
I always mix up left and right.
A랑 B가 헷갈리다 = mix up A and B; the two confusable things take 이/가
출구가 너무 많아서 길이 헷갈렸어요.
There were so many exits that I got confused about the way.
헷갈렸어요 is the past; great for describing getting turned around in a station
이 두 단어가 발음이 비슷해서 자꾸 헷갈려요.
These two words sound similar, so I keep mixing them up.
자꾸 헷갈리다 = keep getting confused; 자꾸 = repeatedly
nuance: 헷갈리다 is the everyday word for things blurring together or getting mixed up — left vs. right, two similar names, which subway exit. It's lighter and more specific than 모르겠어요 (I don't know): you're not clueless, you just can't keep two things straight. Both the experiencer (저는) and the confusing thing (이게) commonly appear with 이/가.
mistakes: Spelling it 햇갈리다 — the first syllable is 헷, not 햇 (a very common typo even among natives)

usage: encouraging someone to just go for it; very common in shops and pep talks
I hesitated for a long while
한참 = for quite a while; pairs naturally with 망설이다
examples: 살까 말까 한참 망설였어요.
I went back and forth for ages on whether to buy it.
V-(으)ㄹ까 말까 망설이다 = waver over whether to do something; the classic indecision pattern
연락할지 말지 계속 망설이고 있어요.
I keep hesitating over whether to reach out.
V-(으)ㄹ지 말지 망설이다 — another way to express dithering about a yes/no choice
망설이다가 결국 기회를 놓쳤어요.
I dithered and ended up missing the chance.
망설이다가 = while hesitating (then something happens); 결국 = in the end
nuance: 망설이다 is hesitating because you can't decide — you waver, you stall, you can't commit. It pairs constantly with -(으)ㄹ까 말까 (whether or not to) to express weighing two options. Compare 고민하다 (to mull over, think hard about a problem): 망설이다 emphasizes the stuck, undecided feeling, while 고민하다 emphasizes the active deliberation.
mistakes: Using 망설이다 for general worrying — for chewing on a problem use 고민하다; 망설이다 is specifically about not being able to decide or act

usage: Decide for yourself / Use your own judgment
스스로 = on one's own; common advice to let someone make the call
겉모습만 보고 = going only by looks; a set phrase about snap judgments
examples: 상황을 보고 판단할게요.
I'll decide based on the situation.
N을/를 보고 판단하다 = judge based on N; the practical 'I'll see and decide' construction
그건 제가 판단할 문제가 아니에요.
That's not for me to judge.
판단할 문제가 아니다 = not a matter for one to decide; useful for stepping back politely
정보가 부족해서 판단하기 어려워요.
There isn't enough information, so it's hard to judge.
판단하기 어렵다 = hard to make a determination; -기 어렵다 turns the verb into 'hard to ~'
nuance: 판단하다 means to assess a situation and form a conclusion or decision — it's more analytical than emotional. It covers both 'judge/evaluate' and 'make a determination,' so it shows up in everything from work decisions to weighing whether something is safe. Unlike English 'judge,' it usually doesn't carry the negative 'being judgmental' sense; for that, Koreans add context like 함부로 판단하다 (to judge rashly).
mistakes: Confusing it with 결정하다 (to decide on a choice) — 판단하다 is the reasoning/assessment that leads to a 결정 (decision)

usage: 예상했던 대로 = as predicted; said when reality matches your forecast
I didn't see it coming at all
예상 못 하다 = fail to anticipate; 전혀 = (not) at all, for total surprise
examples: 주말이라 길이 막힐 거라고 예상했어요.
I expected traffic since it's the weekend.
-(으)ㄹ 거라고 예상하다 = expect that something will happen; the standard 'predict that' frame
생각보다 사람이 많아서 예상이 빗나갔어요.
There were more people than expected, so my prediction was off.
예상이 빗나가다 = a prediction misses; 빗나가다 = to go astray
결과는 어느 정도 예상하고 있었어요.
I'd more or less expected the result.
예상하고 있다 = to be expecting (ongoing); 어느 정도 = to some extent
nuance: 예상하다 is to anticipate or predict an outcome based on reasoning — what you think will happen. It's neutral and works for weather, traffic, exam results, or business forecasts. Distinguish it from 기대하다 (to look forward to / hope for), which carries positive anticipation: you can 예상하다 a bad result, but you wouldn't 기대하다 one.
mistakes: Using 예상하다 when you mean 기대하다 — 예상하다 is a neutral forecast, while 기대하다 implies you're hoping for or excited about it

usage: I had it wrong / I was mistaken
the polite, blame-free way to admit you misremembered or mixed something up
a firm but common way to correct someone's mistaken assumption
examples: 오늘이 토요일인 줄 착각했어요.
I mistakenly thought today was Saturday.
N인 줄 착각하다 = wrongly think that it's N; the key pattern for a mistaken belief
다른 사람으로 착각해서 죄송해요.
Sorry, I mistook you for someone else.
A를 B로 착각하다 = mistake A for B; 으로/로 marks who you confused them with
약속이 내일인 줄 알았는데 착각이었어요.
I thought the appointment was tomorrow, but I was mistaken.
착각이었어요 = it was a mistake (noun form); a natural way to wrap up admitting an error
nuance: 착각하다 is to hold a mistaken belief or impression — you were sure of something that turned out to be wrong (the date, a person's identity, what someone meant). It's about a wrong mental picture, not a clumsy action (that's 실수하다, to slip up). The pattern N인 줄 착각하다 ('wrongly thought it was N') is extremely common and worth memorizing as a chunk.
mistakes: Mixing up 착각하다 with 실수하다 — 착각하다 is thinking something wrong in your head, while 실수하다 is making a careless mistake in action

usage: a direct way to ask if someone suspects you; the object takes 을/를
의심할 여지가 없다 = beyond doubt; a set phrase for total certainty
examples: 처음엔 사기인 줄 알고 의심했어요.
At first I suspected it was a scam.
N인 줄 알고 의심하다 = suspect it's N; very practical for spam calls and shady offers
저는 그 말을 의심하지 않아요.
I don't doubt what they said.
N을/를 의심하다 takes a direct object; here it's 말 (what was said)
자기 자신을 너무 의심하지 마세요.
Don't doubt yourself so much.
자기 자신을 의심하다 = doubt oneself; a kind, encouraging thing to say
nuance: 의심하다 is to doubt or be suspicious of someone or something — you're not sure it's true, honest, or safe. It's transitive (object + 을/를) and ranges from light skepticism about a claim to suspecting a person of wrongdoing. Note it's stronger than just being unsure: 의심하다 implies you actively suspect something is off, which is why it can sound accusatory when aimed at a person.
mistakes: Forgetting the object marker — it's 사람을 의심하다 (suspect a person), not 사람이 의심하다, since 의심하다 is transitive

usage: 짐작이 가다 = to have a hunch; 대충 = roughly. A very natural fixed phrase
It was just as I'd guessed
짐작했던 대로 = as I figured; said when your hunch turns out right
examples: 표정만 봐도 무슨 일인지 짐작할 수 있어요.
I can guess what's going on just from your expression.
N인지 짐작하다 = guess what/whether N is; pairs with 만 봐도 (just by looking)
가격은 어느 정도 짐작하고 있었어요.
I had a rough idea of the price.
짐작하고 있다 = to be guessing/assuming; 어느 정도 = to some degree
왜 그랬는지 짐작도 안 가요.
I can't even begin to guess why they did that.
짐작도 안 가다 = can't even guess; the 도...안 form intensifies 'not at all'
nuance: 짐작하다 is to make an educated guess or surmise based on limited clues — you infer something rather than know it for sure. It's softer and more reasoned than a wild guess: you're reading the signs. The idiom 짐작이 가다 ('a guess comes') is how natives say 'I can imagine / I have a hunch,' and it's far more common in speech than the plain 짐작하다.
mistakes: Using 짐작하다 for a random guess on a quiz — for picking an answer with no basis use 찍다; 짐작하다 implies you're inferring from clues

usage: 떠올려 보다 = try to bring to mind; gentle prompt to jog someone's memory
I can't quite picture the face
note: with 이/가 you'd use the intransitive 떠오르다; use 떠올리다 with 을/를
examples: 그때 기억을 다시 떠올려 봤어요.
I tried to bring back the memory of that time.
N을/를 떠올리다 = call N to mind on purpose; 기억을 떠올리다 = recall a memory
이 사진을 보면 옛날 생각을 떠올리게 돼요.
Looking at this photo makes me recall the old days.
-게 되다 = end up doing; 생각을 떠올리다 = bring a thought to mind
그 사람 이름을 떠올리려고 애썼어요.
I struggled to recall that person's name.
떠올리려고 애쓰다 = strain to remember; 떠올리려고 = trying to bring up
nuance: 떠올리다 is the transitive partner of 떠오르다: you deliberately call a memory, image, or idea to mind (기억을 떠올리다 = you do the recalling), whereas with 떠오르다 the thought surfaces on its own (기억이 떠올라요). Use 떠올리다 + 을/를 when you're the one making the effort to remember. It's warmer and more vivid than 기억하다, which is plain 'to remember/retain.'
mistakes: Swapping it with 떠오르다 — say 생각을 떠올리다 (you actively recall) but 생각이 떠오르다 (it pops up by itself); the particle (을 vs 이) signals which verb you need

usage: 바로 = immediately; describes catching on the instant you sense something
못 알아차리다 = fail to notice; the negative-ability 못 fits this verb naturally
examples: 분위기가 이상한 걸 금방 알아차렸어요.
I quickly picked up that the mood was off.
V-(으)ㄴ 걸 알아차리다 = notice that something is the case; 금방 = in no time
제가 실수한 걸 아무도 못 알아차렸어요.
Nobody noticed that I'd made a mistake.
못 알아차리다 = didn't catch it; great for things that slip past people
뭔가 잘못됐다는 걸 그제야 알아차렸어요.
Only then did I notice something had gone wrong.
그제야 알아차리다 = notice only at that point; -다는 걸 reports what you noticed
nuance: 알아차리다 is to notice or catch on — to suddenly become aware of something through perception (a change in mood, a mistake, someone's true intention). It's about detection, not analysis: you sense it and it registers. Compare 깨닫다 (to realize a fact or truth, often deeper): 알아차리다 is the quicker 'oh, I noticed that,' while 깨닫다 is the heavier 'I came to understand.'
mistakes: Treating it as plain 알다 (to know) — 알아차리다 specifically means the moment of noticing/detecting, not the ongoing state of knowing

usage: I looked back on the past year
a natural year-end reflection phrase; 지난 한 해 = the past year
Sometimes you need to look back
되돌아볼 필요가 있다 = there's a need to reflect; gentle life advice
examples: 한국에서 보낸 시간을 되돌아보면 정말 많이 변했어요.
Looking back on my time in Korea, I've really changed a lot.
N을/를 되돌아보면 = when you look back on N; -보면 sets up a reflective conclusion
힘들 때마다 처음 마음을 되돌아봐요.
Whenever things get hard, I look back on how I felt at the start.
처음 마음을 되돌아보다 = revisit your original feelings/intentions; 마다 = every time
실수를 되돌아보고 다음엔 더 잘하려고 해요.
I reflect on my mistakes and try to do better next time.
되돌아보고 = reflect and then; pairs with -(으)려고 하다 (intend to)
nuance: 되돌아보다 is to reflect on or look back over the past — your year, your choices, a relationship — usually to draw a lesson or feeling from it. The 되- prefix adds a 'back again' nuance, making it more reflective than plain 돌아보다 (to turn and look). It's an introspective, slightly thoughtful word, perfect for journaling, year-end musings, or talking about how you've grown.
mistakes: Using it for physically turning your head to look behind — that's 돌아보다 or 뒤를 돌아보다; 되돌아보다 is overwhelmingly about reflecting on the past
